{{Short description|American cell biologist}}

[[file:RayRappaport.jpg|right|thumb|Ray and Barbara Rappaport in 1989]]
'''Ray Rappaport''' (May 21, 1922 – December 14, 2010) was an American [[cell biologist]]. He did pioneering research using physical manipulations of cells to understand the mechanisms of [[cytokinesis]], the process by which a cell's cytoplasm is divided in two.

Raymond Rappaport was born in May 1922 in North Bergen, New Jersey, to Raymond and Verna Karper Rappaport.<ref name="obituary">''Bangor Daily News'', December 17, 2010, "[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bangordailynews/obituary.aspx?n=raymond-rappaport&pid=147178519]"</ref> He attended [[Bethany College (West Virginia)]]. His studies were interrupted by service during [[World War II]] in the 5th Service Command, Anti-Aircraft and then in the Army Medical Corps. He finished his undergraduate work at [[Columbia University]], and enrolled in a masters program in Zoology at the [[University of Michigan]]. In a soil microbiology course, he met fellow masters student Barbara Nolan, and the two were wed in 1947. He earned his master's degree in 1948, and a PhD from [[Yale University]] in 1952.<ref name="retirement">''Schenectady Gazette'', July 13, 1987, "[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=0g8hAAAAIBAJ&sjid=inIFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3731,3154539&dq=raymond-rappaport+union-college&hl=en]"</ref>

Rappaport began his career as a professor at [[Union College]] in Schenectady, New York in 1952.<ref name="retirement" /> He taught for 35 years and conducted research at the college and for most summers at [[MDI Biological Laboratory]] in Salisbury Cove, Maine. Rappaport held several administrative positions at the MDI Biological Laboratory, including director (1956–1959), trustee, and president of the corporation (1979–1981).<ref name="obituary" /><ref name="Henson Shuster">Henson J.H, Shuster C.B ''The Bulletin of the Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory'', volume 50, 2011, "[http://mdibl.org/bulletin/bulletin_2011.pdf]" accessed August 27, 2015</ref> Rappaport also architecturally designed some of the buildings at the laboratory, including several cottages, laboratory buildings, and the dining hall.<ref name="aaaselection">''Bangor Daily News'', June 23, 1983, "[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Wh00AAAAIBAJ&sjid=8OAIAAAAIBAJ&pg=5001,2896690&dq=raymond-rappaport&hl=en]"</ref><ref name="Henson Shuster" /> He and his wife retired to Maine in 1987, where he continued research year-round at MDIBL.<ref name="retirement" />

Most of Rappaport's research made use of [[echinoderm]] embryonic cells to address the mechanisms of [[cytokinesis]] in animal cells, experiments that focused on understanding how the cytokinetic furrow is positioned, and understanding the nature of the stimulus from the [[mitotic spindle]] that induced cortical furrowing.<ref name="pollard">''Ray Rappaport Chronology: Twenty-Five Years of Seminal Papers on Cytokinesis in the Journal of Experimental Zoology'', by Thomas D. Pollard, J Exp Zool 301A:9-14 (2004)</ref> With few exceptions, his research was conducted alone or with his wife.<ref name="pollard" /> Rappaport's research was marked by unusually creative and simple experimental design, often involving physical manipulation of individual cells, for which he devised a number of custom microsurgical tools.<ref name="obituary" /><ref name="retirement" /><ref name="pollard" /> Rappaport recognized mechanistic redundancy in cytokinesis, which he characterized in an address at a 2004 conference with, "When I began working on cytokinesis, I thought I was tinkering with a beautifully made Swiss watch, but what I was really working on was an old Maine fishing boat engine: overbuilt, inefficient, never-failed and repaired by simple measures."<ref name="Henson Shuster" />

Rappaport died December 14, 2010, in [[Bar Harbor, Maine]], at the age of 88.<ref name="obituary" />

== Honors and awards ==
Rappaport was elected as a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1983.<ref name="aaaselection" /> A laboratory building at MDIBL is named after him.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://mdibl.org/laboratory/rappaport/ |archive-date=Sep 18, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150918024919/http://mdibl.org/laboratory/rappaport/ |title=Rappaport Laboratory |website=[[MDI Biological Laboratory]] |access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref>
